Situation1: They are expected to be present at a family dinner or small gathering.
Expectation2: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation2: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Story:
I was just about to sit down at the dinner table, the smell of my mom’s cooking filling the house, when my phone buzzed. My family had been looking forward to this dinner all week—my parents kept saying how important it was for us all to be together, especially since I’d been so busy lately. As I took my seat, I glanced at my phone and saw a string of frantic messages from my best friend, Sam. His car had broken down on the highway, miles from home, and he sounded scared. He needed me to come get him right away.

My dad was already pouring drinks, my little sister was telling a story, and everyone was waiting for me to join in. But Sam was out there alone, in the dark, counting on me. I could feel my heart pounding as I looked from my family to my phone, torn between the warmth of home and the urgent call for help. I knew both sides expected me to be there for them, but I couldn’t be in two places at once. The weight of their expectations pressed down on me, and I sat frozen, unsure of what to do next.
